entries.name: Fairstead Capital Management LLC, et al. v. Blodgett

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Fairstead's lead argument that the de facto stay and the Damages-Phase Scheduling Order mooted the fact-discovery cutoff (and excused the expert timing): rejected; deferring trial did not set aside completed phases, no one acted as if fact discovery reopened, and expert disclosure had already been made before the trial deferral.

Fairstead's argument that the Damages-Phase Scheduling Order's call for "materials relied upon by Expert and not produced previously by parties" and the "natural course" of expert work authorized the production: rejected; that language covers materials never requested or publicly available, and cannot be used to redo fact discovery on previously requested documents.

Fairstead's argument that it reserved a "right to supplement and amend" its expert designation: rejected under Goldstein; even a mutual reservation cannot amend a scheduling order, and a unilateral one is "a contumacious nullity." Its related claim that the General Scheduling Order permits amendment by written agreement failed because there was no written agreement and, per Encite, counsel's agreement has no effect until the court adopts it (fn. 55).

Fairstead's contention, citing Dole and Merion Capital, that Delaware law permits expert swapping: rejected; Dole involved substituting the natural person who wrote the report for his firm with no change in opinions, and Fairstead's Merion quotation omitted the limiting phrase "as a result of illness" (fn. 53 cites Leiske on mischaracterized authority).

Fairstead's explanation that Dunec's apprehension (and, in its opposition, a scheduling conflict) justified the swap: waived because first disclosed at oral argument, depriving Blodgett of a chance to respond (Candlewood); regardless, an expert's vague uneasiness is not good cause.

Fairstead's argument that Blodgett's evolving damages theories required new experts: rejected; Blodgett's theories did not change, and his report narrowed the projects at issue and relied on collateral estoppel, making response easier.

Fairstead's argument that the swap "changed only the name on the report," caused no prejudice, and could be cured by depositions and a reply report: rejected; the swap would erase the Tatum record and the Court's comments on Dunec, give Fairstead a second bite at valuation, compress Blodgett's time, and delay the case.

Fairstead's argument that Concord and Drejka require a broader balancing before preclusion and that preclusion here is case-terminating: rejected; Concord's balancing fits within Rule 6(b) good cause (and favored exclusion there), Drejka applies only to case-terminating sanctions, and Fairstead does not bear the burden of proof and retains its timely experts.

Fairstead's "trump card" reading of Christian that Blodgett waived enforcement by not promptly raising non-compliance: rejected; Christian addressed a specific personal-injury practice in Superior Court and did not silently abrogate Rule 6 or trial courts' docket discretion.

Fairstead's arguments that "sufficient to show" requests let it produce a limited set and supplement later, that Blodgett's expert did not run distribution waterfalls, and that RFP 47 was vague because "Feldman" was undefined: rejected; Blodgett was entitled to rely on Fairstead's sufficiency representation and its relevance-only objection, and the vagueness objection was not made originally and is "frivolous."

authorities_cited.authority: Ct. Ch. R. 6(b)
authorities_cited.proposition: Onus is on the party missing or anticipating missing a deadline; post-deadline relief requires a motion, excusable neglect and good cause.

authorities_cited.authority: Coleman v. PricewaterhouseCoopers, LLC, 902 A.2d 1102 (Del. 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: Good cause is likely found where the movant was generally diligent, the need was neither foreseeable nor its fault, and denial risks substantial unfairness.

authorities_cited.authority: Encite LLC v. Soni, 2011 WL 1565181 (Del. Ch. Apr. 15, 2011)
authorities_cited.proposition: Belief in an informal extension is not excusable neglect; disclosing an expert after reviewing the opponent's report is an unfair advantage; delay and even mild prejudice weigh against good cause; counsel's agreement has no effect until the court adopts it.

authorities_cited.authority: Candlewood Timber Gp. LLC v. Pan Am. Energy LLC, 2006 WL 258305 (Del. Super. Jan. 18, 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: Substitute expert precluded where unavailability was unexplained until oral argument, depriving the opponent of a chance to respond.

authorities_cited.authority: Goldstein v. Denner, 2024 WL 1599501 (Del. Ch. Apr. 1, 2024) (ORDER)
authorities_cited.proposition: A reservation of rights to add witnesses cannot amend a scheduling order; the late-disclosing party must show excusable neglect.

authorities_cited.authority: S'holder Representative Servs., LLC v. Alexion Pharms., Inc., 2023 WL 2632477 (Del. Ch. Mar. 23, 2023) (ORDER)
authorities_cited.proposition: "Deadlines matter"; expert excluded for a six-day-late disclosure absent a pre-deadline extension or excusable neglect.

authorities_cited.authority: Strong v. Chae, 2024 WL 4583092 (Del. Ch. Oct. 23, 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: An untimely disclosed expert's report excluded and testimony barred on that basis alone.

authorities_cited.authority: Concord Towers, Inc. v. Long, 348 A.2d 325 (Del. 1975)
authorities_cited.proposition: Balancing the duty to admit relevant evidence against fairness and the Rules fits within Rule 6(b) good cause and there favored exclusion.

authorities_cited.authority: IQ Hldgs., Inc. v. Am. Com. Lines Inc., 2012 WL 3877790 (Del. Ch. Aug. 30, 2012)
authorities_cited.proposition: Delaware courts strictly adhere to discovery cutoffs; late production is grounds for exclusion.

authorities_cited.authority: In re ExamWorks Gp., Inc. S'holder Appraisal Litig., 2018 WL 1008439 (Del. Ch. Feb. 21, 2018)
authorities_cited.proposition: Scheduling orders have the force of court orders; disregarding discovery provisions is discovery abuse; counsel who fail to communicate about missed deadlines shirk their obligations.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Asbestos Litig., 228 A.3d 676 (Del. 2020)
authorities_cited.proposition: Good cause governs modification of scheduling deadlines; Christian cited only for the abuse-of-discretion standard, without its waiver rule.

authorities_cited.authority: Holt v. Holt, 472 A.2d 820 (Del. 1984)
authorities_cited.proposition: Discovery abuse has no place in Delaware courts; trial courts must take prompt corrective action.

authorities_cited.authority: Drejka v. Hitchens Tire Serv. Inc., 15 A.3d 1221 (Del. 2010)
authorities_cited.proposition: Multi-factor default-judgment balancing applies only when a court considers a case-terminating sanction, not to the excusable-neglect/good-cause inquiry.

authorities_cited.authority: Christian v. Counseling Res. Assocs., Inc., 60 A.3d 1083 (Del. 2013)
authorities_cited.proposition: Waiver rule for failing to promptly raise an opponent's scheduling violations addressed a specific personal-injury practice in Superior Court and is not a universal rule.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Dole Food Co., Inc. S'holder Litig., 110 A.3d 1257 (Del. Ch. 2015)
authorities_cited.proposition: Substitution allowed only where the natural person who prepared the report adopted it, with no change in testifier or opinions.

authorities_cited.authority: Merion Cap., L.P. v. 3M Cogent, Inc., 2013 WL 3793896 (Del. Ch. July 8, 2013)
authorities_cited.proposition: An expert can generally replace one who must drop out as a result of illness; no illness was claimed.

authorities_cited.authority: Moses v. Drake, 109 A.3d 562 (Del. 2015)
authorities_cited.proposition: Affirmed refusal to consider late supplemental expert reports without discussing Christian's waiver rule or Drejka.

authorities_cited.authority: Hoag v. Amex Assurance Co., 953 A.2d 713 (Del. 2008)
authorities_cited.proposition: Trial courts should diligently impose discovery sanctions to penalize and deter.

authorities_cited.authority: Terramar Retail Ctrs. LLC v. Marion #2-Seaport Tr., 2018 WL 6331622 (Del. Ch. Dec. 4, 2018)
authorities_cited.proposition: Preclusion warranted as a sanction.

authorities_cited.authority: Leiske v. Kidd, 2026 WL 3459553 (Del. Ch. Nov. 13, 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: Signing attorneys must ensure cited authorities support the propositions cited, whatever the source of error.

authorities_cited.authority: Wright v. SLWM, LLC, 341 A.3d 551 (Del. Ch. 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: A party claiming vagueness must identify the ambiguity and explain its interpretation.

authorities_cited.authority: Solow v. Aspect Res., LLC, 46 A.3d 1074 (Del. 2012); Sammons v. Drs. for Emergency Servs., P.A., 913 A.2d 519 (Del. 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: Trial courts have inherent power and discretion to control their dockets.

authorities_cited.authority: Ct. Ch. R. 1
authorities_cited.proposition: Just, speedy and inexpensive determination of every proceeding.

summary.brief_summary: After granting summary judgment that the LLCs improperly forfeited William Blodgett's interests, the Court of Chancery (Laster, V.C.) addressed Blodgett's motion to preclude Fairstead from relying in the damages phase on newly swapped-in experts and on ~2,400 pages produced years after the fact-discovery cutoff. Applying Rule 6(b), the Court held that Fairstead never sought relief or showed excusable neglect or good cause, made the swap only after seeing Blodgett's report (and after Tatum discredited its expert Dunec), and could not use the expert-reliance clause to produce documents Blodgett requested in 2023. The Court confined Concord to the good-cause inquiry, Drejka to case-terminating sanctions, and Christian to its personal-injury context.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether Fairstead, at the damages phase after summary judgment for Blodgett, could (i) replace its two July 2024 experts with new experts disclosed more than two years after the General Scheduling Order's expert-identification deadline and after seeing Blodgett's opening report, and (ii) rely on ~2,400 pages produced long after the June 14, 2024 fact-discovery cutoff, without moving under Ct. Ch. R. 6(b) and showing excusable neglect and good cause; and whether Concord, Drejka or Christian displace that framework.
summary.holding: Motion to preclude granted. Fairstead may not rely on the experts disclosed in August and September 2026 (Kopa, Lee, Aaron, Kincer) and may rely only on its July 2024 experts; it also may not rely on the August 8, 2026 Additional Materials. The Court held the swap violated the General Scheduling Order's July 26, 2024 expert-identification deadline, which neither scheduling order contemplated revisiting, and that Fairstead never moved under Rule 6(b) or argued excusable neglect or good cause. Its shifting, after-the-fact justifications failed, and the Court found its silence apparently tactical and its conduct worse than in prior preclusion cases; a lesser sanction would reward that silence and delay. The production violated the fact-discovery cutoff because Blodgett's 2023 requests called for the documents; the expert-reliance clause cannot reopen fact discovery, and Fairstead is bound by its "sufficient to show" production and its relevance-only objection to RFP 47. The Court characterized the late production as "abusive." Concord fits within the good-cause analysis; Drejka applies only to case-terminating sanctions, which this is not; Christian is confined to its personal-injury context and did not abrogate Rule 6. Within ten days the parties must submit an agreed schedule to conclude the matter or, failing agreement, a joint letter of up to 3,000 words with competing forms of order.
key_facts_and_concessions: The General Scheduling Order memorialized the June 14, 2024 fact-discovery cutoff and required expert identification on July 26, 2024; Fairstead timely identified Scott Drago and Mark Dunec, the same experts it used in the factually overlapping Tatum case.

In October 2024 the parties agreed to defer trial until after the arbitration and Tatum and to "extend the schedule for expert discovery consistent with any deferral of the trial date"; no one proposed reopening fact discovery or re-identifying experts, and the case was never formally stayed.

The October 2025 Tatum post-trial decision rejected Dunec's valuation; with that decision in hand, Fairstead's June 2026 joint-letter position proposed neither more fact discovery nor new experts, and Fairstead agreed to the Damages-Phase Scheduling Order without mentioning any expert change or additional production.

On Saturday, August 8, 2026, four business days before Blodgett's opening report was due, Fairstead produced ~2,400 pages (governance agreements, 2015-2023 financials, membership interest purchase agreements, tax returns, and a spreadsheet of expenditures Feldman claimed were capital contributions), which the Court found was precisely what Blodgett requested in April 2023.

Fairstead had objected to RFP 47 (Feldman's capital contributions) solely on relevance grounds, and had represented that all documents responsive to Blodgett's NYS8 Portfolio valuation follow-up had been produced.

On August 17, 2026, three days after Blodgett's opening report, Fairstead served an unexplained "amended" disclosure replacing Drago and Dunec with Kopa, Lee and Aaron; after Blodgett moved to preclude, it replaced Aaron with Kincer on September 3.

Fairstead never moved to amend either scheduling order and did not argue excusable neglect or good cause for the experts or the production; the Court treated this as an implicit concession that Fairstead cannot satisfy either standard for the production.
Only at oral argument did Fairstead say Dunec had grown concerned about testifying after the Tatum decision; it never said he could not or would not testify, only that he preferred not to.
summary.practical_takeaway: A party that needs to change a disclosed expert or rely on documents an opponent requested during fact discovery should raise it with opposing counsel promptly, document any agreement by stipulation submitted for court approval, and otherwise move under Rule 6(b) before acting. Reservations of rights and expert-reliance production clauses will not cure a missed deadline, and a responding party will be held to its "sufficient to show" production and its stated objections.
summary.standard_of_review: Ct. Ch. R. 6(b): a party that has missed a court-ordered deadline must move for relief, show excusable neglect, and show good cause (a legitimate, sufficient and persuasive reason, assessed by diligence, whether the need was foreseeable or the movant's fault, and risk of unfairness to the movant; prejudice to the other side may be considered, but its absence alone is not good cause). Facts drawn from the motion submissions, not formal findings.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Freiberg's argument that his "meritorious prosecution" of the Section 225 action caused the curative action (the McFadden Consents) and produced judicial certainty about Xonar's board: rejected. The Court found his motion overstates the Post-Trial Opinion, so it is not certain he conferred any corporate benefit.

Freiberg's argument that the suit "exposed" an incorrect capitalization table: rejected. The Post-Trial Opinion expressly did not address how the capitalization table should be calculated or whether it was incorrect.
Freiberg's argument that the suit showed the original written consents were not effective when executed: rejected. The Post-Trial Opinion found the consents effective on January 27 at the latest.

Freiberg's argument that the McFadden Consents were needed to "cure a deficiency in a stockholder action that [Xonar] had been treating as valid": rejected, because the Post-Trial Opinion did not definitively so conclude.

Freiberg's request for fees as a matter of the Court's equitable discretion: rejected. As in Keyser, Freiberg was principally motivated to benefit himself by confirming his board seat, not to benefit Xonar.

authorities_cited.authority: Keyser v. Curtis, 2012 WL 3115453 (Del. Ch. July 31, 2012), aff'd on other grounds sub nom. Poliak v. Keyser, 65 A.3d 617 (Del. 2013)
authorities_cited.proposition: Even prevailing Section 225 plaintiffs who conferred some benefit (certainty on share ownership and an invalid issuance) were denied fees because they, not the company, were the principal beneficiaries. Suing to confirm a board seat is not wrong, but it does not call for a fee award.

authorities_cited.authority: CCSB Fin. Corp. v. Totta, 302 A.3d 387 (Del. 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: The general rule in Section 225 actions is that the benefit runs to the individuals seeking to confirm their board seats, so fees ordinarily should not be awarded.

authorities_cited.authority: Judy v. Preferred Commc'n Sys., Inc., 2016 WL 4992687 (Del. Ch. Sept. 19, 2016)
authorities_cited.proposition: The Court may decline fees even if the prerequisites are technically met, considering divergence of interests and public policy. A litigant whose primary purpose is to advance personal interests lacks standing to obtain a fee award.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Orchard Enters., Inc. S'holder Litig., 2014 WL 4181912 (Del. Ch. Aug. 22, 2014)
authorities_cited.proposition: The corporate benefit prerequisites are necessary but not sufficient for a fee award.

authorities_cited.authority: Frank v. Elgamal, 2011 WL 3300344 (Del. Ch. July 28, 2011)
authorities_cited.proposition: Whether to award attorneys' fees is committed to the Court's discretion.

authorities_cited.authority: Hollywood Firefighters' Pension Fund v. Malone, 2021 WL 5179219 (Del. Ch. Nov. 8, 2021)
authorities_cited.proposition: States the three-part test for fees based on a corporate benefit that moots a lawsuit.

authorities_cited.authority: United Vanguard Fund, Inc. v. TakeCare, Inc., 693 A.2d 1076 (Del. 1997)
authorities_cited.proposition: Source of the three-part mootness fee test, quoted through Hollywood Firefighters.

authorities_cited.authority: Freiberg v. Xonar Tech. Inc., 2026 WL 2719136 (Del. Ch. Sept. 15, 2026) (Post-Trial Opinion)
authorities_cited.proposition: Did not reach the capitalization-table methodology and found the consents effective on January 27 at the latest, which undercuts Freiberg's claimed benefit.

authorities_cited.authority: Corporate benefit doctrine
authorities_cited.proposition: Equitable exception to the American Rule, invoked by Freiberg and held inapplicable.

authorities_cited.authority: Montgomery Cellular Hldg. Co. v. Dobler, 880 A.2d 206 (Del. 2005)
authorities_cited.proposition: Delaware follows the American Rule: each side bears its own fees.

authorities_cited.authority: EMAK Worldwide, Inc. v. Kurz, 50 A.3d 429 (Del. 2012)
authorities_cited.proposition: The corporate benefit doctrine is an equitable exception to the American Rule.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Dunkin' Donuts S'holders Litig., 1990 WL 189120 (Del. Ch. Nov. 27, 1990)
authorities_cited.proposition: Cited through Frank and Judy for fee discretion and for declining fees despite satisfied prerequisites.

authorities_cited.authority: Mentor Graphics Corp. v. Quickturn Design Sys., Inc., 789 A.2d 1216 (Del. Ch. 2001), aff'd sub nom. Mentor Graphics Corp. v. Shapiro, 818 A.2d 959 (Del. 2003)
authorities_cited.proposition: Cited through Judy on declining fees where the litigant's interests diverge from those it purports to benefit.
Summary proceeding Freiberg used to challenge his board removal.

summary.brief_summary: After losing his Section 225 challenge to his removal from Xonar Technology Inc.'s board in a post-trial decision, Gregory Freiberg sought fees under the corporate benefit doctrine. He argued that his suit caused Xonar to obtain the curative McFadden Consents and produced certainty about the board's composition. Chancellor McCormick denied the motion: Freiberg overstated what the Post-Trial Opinion decided, so any corporate benefit was uncertain. In any event, as in Keyser, a Section 225 litigant suing to confirm his own board seat is the principal beneficiary, and his litigation conduct showed a personal motive. Costs were also denied because he did not prevail. (The caption supplied spells the name "Frieberg"; the opinion uses "Freiberg.")
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether a director who lost his 8 Del. C. § 225 challenge to his removal by stockholder written consent may still recover attorneys' fees and expenses under the corporate benefit doctrine, on the theory that his suit caused Xonar to obtain curative consents (the McFadden Consents) and so produced certainty about the board's composition.

flags.evidence: the Post-Trial Opinion found they were "effective on January 27 at the latest." Footnote 9: "Id. at *10–11 (emphasis added)."
flags.opinion_says: The quote is accurate, but the footnote says the emphasis was added by the Court in this letter, not that it appears in the original.
flags.problem: The footnote says "emphasis added," so the emphasis was not in the original Post-Trial Opinion.

summary.holding: Freiberg's motion for attorneys' fees and expenses is denied. First, it is not certain he conferred any corporate benefit. His motion overstates the Post-Trial Opinion, which did not decide whether the capitalization table was wrong, found the consents effective on January 27 at the latest, and did not definitively find that the McFadden Consents cured a deficiency. Second, even if the prerequisites were met, the Court exercised its discretion to deny fees. Following Keyser and the general rule in CCSB v. Totta, Freiberg was principally motivated to benefit himself by confirming his board seat. The Court found that motive evident from his pursuit of expansive discovery beyond the scope of the summary action and his refusal to stipulate to his own version of the capitalization table when Xonar offered to streamline. The Court also held Freiberg is not entitled to costs because he was not the prevailing party.
key_facts_and_concessions: The Post-Trial Opinion (Sept. 15, 2026) held that Freiberg failed to establish that the McFadden Consents should not count toward his removal. It therefore did not reach the second triable issue, the methodology for calculating his share ownership, and held that his removal was not improper.
Freiberg acknowledged that he needed to win on both triable issues to prevail.

Solely for purposes of the Section 225 dispute, Xonar stipulated to accept Freiberg's allegations and his version of the capitalization table, with two exceptions: whether the McFadden Consents count, and the share-ownership methodology.

The Post-Trial Opinion found the consents "effective on January 27 at the latest" (emphasis in original). It did not decide whether the capitalization table was incorrect or whether the McFadden Consents were necessary to cure a deficiency.
After Freiberg filed suit challenging his January 2026 removal, Xonar obtained additional written consents from stockholders Brian and Jeff McFadden.

Per the Court, Freiberg "aggressively pursued expansive discovery beyond the scope of this summary action." The Court also found that he "refused to stipulate to his own version of the capitalization table when Xonar offered to streamline proceedings."
Freiberg sued in hopes of confirming his board seat.
summary.practical_takeaway: In Section 225 litigation, a fee claim under the corporate benefit doctrine faces a strong presumption against fees because the benefit is presumed to run to the would-be director. A fee motion must track precisely what the merits decision actually held, because claiming a benefit the Court never found undermines the request. Litigation conduct suggesting personal motive, such as discovery beyond the summary proceeding's scope or rejecting offers to streamline, will be weighed against a discretionary award.
summary.standard_of_review: Corporate benefit exception to the American Rule. For a benefit that moots a suit, plaintiff must show (1) the suit was meritorious when filed, (2) defendants took the beneficial action before judicial resolution, and (3) the benefit was causally related to the suit. These prerequisites are necessary but not sufficient, and the fee decision is committed to the Court's discretion.

entries.name: Golden Rule Fin. Corp. v. S'holder Representative Servs., LLC

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Golden Rule's principal argument that SRS should not receive prejudgment interest on amounts obtained through breaches for which SRS is liable: rejected. It conflates the Section 3.4(a) payment obligation with the Article IX indemnification right; the two rulings address different contractual rights, so there is no compelling reason under the law of the case to revise.

Golden Rule's argument that interest it pays SRS on the breach-attributable portion is itself an indemnifiable "Loss" under § 9.2(a), so that paying it now creates a "daisy-chain": rejected. The Memorandum Opinion did not hold SRS's interest award to be a Loss, and that interest originated from Golden Rule's payment delay, not from USHEALTH's breaches. Arwood was distinguished.

Golden Rule's argument that the Summary Judgment Order awarded delay damages rather than prejudgment interest because the principal claim was mooted: rejected. The Summary Judgment Ruling awarded prejudgment interest as a matter of right, which Golden Rule had not disputed.

Golden Rule's request for equitable offset under Reddy: rejected. SRS's interest award (for Golden Rule's payment delay) and Golden Rule's indemnification judgment are related but not identical, so offset would not merely eliminate a superfluous exchange but would extinguish a separately adjudicated award.

Golden Rule's argument that the equities demand offset because the remaining Escrow Funds cannot satisfy its judgment: rejected. Offset would reduce an independent obligation owed to SRS and circumvent the Merger Agreement's limitation of indemnification recovery to the Escrow Funds.
Golden Rule's argument that SRS's litigation conduct warrants offset: rejected as unpersuasive for the same contractual-mechanics reasons.

Golden Rule's argument that the denial of Rule 54(b) certification signaled a predisposition to revise the interest award later: rejected. The Court did not reserve SRS's interest entitlement; it denied certification because SRS had not shown the infrequent and harsh case warranting immediate partial final judgment.

Golden Rule's argument that the denial of certification reflected a "reasonable chance that the claims for fees or interest could offset one another": rejected. The Court never indicated offset was possible, and the denial merely preserved authority to revisit the order if warranted.

SRS's argument that Golden Rule's position cannot be reconciled with the Memorandum Opinion's res judicata ruling: rejected as lacking merit. SRS's interest entitlement arose from Golden Rule's delayed Section 3.4(a) payment asserted in Counterclaim I, not from the Prior Action, so the res judicata ruling is not implicated.

authorities_cited.authority: Ct. Ch. R. 54(b)
authorities_cited.proposition: Permits partial final judgment, and permits revision of an order adjudicating fewer than all claims at any time before final judgment.

authorities_cited.authority: Merger Agreement §§ 3.4(a), 9.2(a), 9.3(b)-(c)
authorities_cited.proposition: Separates the true-up payment obligation from indemnification for Losses, and makes the Escrow Funds the cap, sole source of recovery and exclusive remedy for indemnification.

authorities_cited.authority: Tornetta v. Musk, 326 A.3d 1203 (Del. Ch. 2024), rev'd on other grounds sub nom. In re Tesla, Inc. Deriv. Litig., 351 A.3d 1005 (Del. 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: The law of the case doctrine supplies the standard for revising interlocutory orders under Rule 54(b).

authorities_cited.authority: Taylor v. Jones, 2006 WL 1510437 (Del. Ch. May 25, 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: Issues already decided will not be disturbed by the same court absent a compelling reason.

authorities_cited.authority: Gannett Co., Inc. v. Kanaga, 750 A.2d 1174 (Del. 2000)
authorities_cited.proposition: Law of the case does not bar reconsideration of a ruling that is clearly wrong, produces an injustice, or should be revisited because of changed circumstances.

authorities_cited.authority: Brandywine Smyrna, Inc. v. Millennium Builders, LLC, 34 A.3d 482 (Del. 2011)
authorities_cited.proposition: Prejudgment interest is awarded as of right, compensates for loss of use of money, forces disgorgement of the benefit of retention, and accrues from the date payment was due.

authorities_cited.authority: Pettinaro Constr. Co., Inc. v. Lindh, 428 A.2d 1161 (Del. 1981)
authorities_cited.proposition: Set-off is allowed only when equity and good conscience require it, substantial justice is promoted, and third-party rights are not infringed.

authorities_cited.authority: FdG Logistics LLC v. A&R Logistics Holdings, Inc., 131 A.3d 842 (Del. Ch. 2016), aff'd, 148 A.3d 1171 (Del. 2016) (TABLE)
authorities_cited.proposition: A sophisticated buyer that did not bargain for a right to delay payment pending indemnification claims must pay when due.

authorities_cited.authority: New Enter. Assocs. 14, L.P. v. Rich, 295 A.3d 520 (Del. Ch. 2023) (quoting Abry P'rs V, L.P. v. F & W Acq. LLC, 891 A.2d 1032 (Del. Ch. 2006))
authorities_cited.proposition: Delaware courts are especially chary about relieving sophisticated entities of freely negotiated contracts.

authorities_cited.authority: Totta v. CCSB Fin. Corp., 2022 WL 4087800 (Del. Ch. Sep. 7, 2022)
authorities_cited.proposition: A pending attorneys' fees petition does not foreclose Rule 54(b) partial final judgment.

authorities_cited.authority: Marilyn Abrams Living Tr. v. Pope Invs. LLC, 188 A.3d 829 (Del. Ch. 2018)
authorities_cited.proposition: A trial court may defer a fee ruling until after the merits appeal only if it certifies the merits ruling under Rule 54(b).

authorities_cited.authority: 80 C.J.S. Set-off and Counterclaim § 5 (2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: Set-off applies mutual debts against each other and generally eliminates a superfluous exchange of money.

authorities_cited.authority: Arwood v. AW Site Services, LLC, 2022 WL 973441 (Del. Ch. Mar. 31, 2022)
authorities_cited.proposition: Held that prejudgment interest and costs fell within a contractual "Losses" definition and could not exceed an exhausted cap. Distinguished because it involved the same recovering party, not a separately adjudicated interest award to the opposing party.

authorities_cited.authority: Reddy v. PrimeCare International, Inc., 2000 WL 1654834 (Del. Ch. Oct. 20, 2000)
authorities_cited.proposition: Offset was appropriate where advancement and reimbursement obligations were identical and circular. Distinguished because the obligations here are related but not identical.

authorities_cited.authority: Emerald P'rs v. Berlin, 811 A.2d 788 (Del. 2001)
authorities_cited.proposition: A merits judgment is not final until an outstanding fee application is decided.

authorities_cited.authority: Tyson Foods, Inc. v. Aetos Corp., 809 A.2d 575 (Del. 2002)
authorities_cited.proposition: Definition of final judgment; interlocutory rulings are reviewed through appeal of the final order.

authorities_cited.authority: DeMatteis v. RiseDelaware Inc., 315 A.3d 499 (Del. 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: Merger rule: interlocutory orders merge into the final judgment.

authorities_cited.authority: State v. Wright, 131 A.3d 310 (Del. 2016)
authorities_cited.proposition: Law of the case promotes efficiency, finality and stability.

authorities_cited.authority: C. v. C., 320 A.2d 717 (Del. 1974); Frank G.W. v. Carol M.W., 457 A.2d 715 (Del. 1983)
authorities_cited.proposition: An interlocutory judgment remains within the court's control until final judgment.

authorities_cited.authority: Campbell v. Caravel Acad., Inc., 1989 WL 25804 (Del. Ch. Mar. 16, 1989)
authorities_cited.proposition: Costs and fees are best addressed after the appellate process.

summary.brief_summary: After a post-trial Memorandum Opinion awarded Golden Rule Financial Corp. $38.3 million in indemnifiable Losses against Shareholder Representative Services LLC (SRS), the parties submitted competing Rule 54(b) implementing orders. They disagreed over whether the Court's earlier, uncertified Summary Judgment Order awarding SRS prejudgment interest (about $7.2 million through June 16, 2023, plus continuing interest) on Golden Rule's delayed payment of the Final Adjustment Amount should be cut back or offset. Vice Chancellor Fioravanti applied law of the case principles to the request to revise the interlocutory order. The Court held that the interest award rested on Golden Rule's Section 3.4(a) payment delay, a right distinct from Golden Rule's Article IX indemnification claim, so it was neither an indemnifiable Loss nor a proper subject of equitable offset given the Merger Agreement's escrow-only exclusive remedy, and it adopted SRS's form of order.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether, in implementing a post-trial indemnification judgment for Golden Rule under Article IX of the Merger Agreement, the Court should revise its interlocutory Summary Judgment Order awarding SRS prejudgment interest on Golden Rule's delayed Section 3.4(a) payment of the Final Adjustment Amount, either by limiting that interest to the portion not attributable to USHEALTH's breaches, treating it as an indemnifiable Loss, or offsetting it against Golden Rule's judgment.
summary.holding: Golden Rule's proposed implementing order is denied, and SRS's proposed partial final judgment under Rule 54(b) is granted. Because there is no just reason to delay judgment on the resolved merits issues, the Court enters partial final judgment and leaves fees and costs for later determination, as both sides proposed. Golden Rule's proposal would revise the interlocutory Summary Judgment Order, and the Court held that law of the case principles govern such a revision and that Golden Rule showed no compelling reason for one. The Summary Judgment Order compensated SRS for Golden Rule's delay in paying the Final Adjustment Amount under Section 3.4(a), whereas the Memorandum Opinion adjudicated a distinct Article IX indemnification right. SRS's interest is therefore neither a Losses component nor subject to equitable offset. Offset would extinguish a separately adjudicated award and circumvent the escrow-only exclusive remedy, and Golden Rule could have bargained for, but did not obtain, a right to delay the true-up pending indemnification claims. SRS's res judicata argument was also rejected as not implicated. The judgment is for Golden Rule on Counts I and II: $38,342,458 in damages plus $14,614,103 in prejudgment interest from January 25, 2023, totaling $52,956,561, with the Summary Judgment Order's interest award to SRS incorporated undisturbed. The parties are directed to submit a revised order consistent with the decision.
key_facts_and_concessions: The Summary Judgment Order awarded SRS prejudgment interest on Counterclaim I "from May 18, 2020 through June 16, 2023 in the amount of $7,219,340," with interest continuing to accrue on that sum at the legal rate, compounded quarterly, until payment. May 18, 2020 is the date Golden Rule filed the Prior Action.
The Court denied Rule 54(b) certification of the Summary Judgment Order, so that order remained interlocutory and subject to revision before final judgment.
Golden Rule paid the $40,164,358.82 Final Adjustment Amount on January 25, 2023, before summary judgment argument, mooting SRS's request for the principal.
In opposing summary judgment, Golden Rule did not contest SRS's right to prejudgment interest and disputed only when it began to accrue.

The Memorandum Opinion found an indemnifiable Loss of $38.3 million against SRS for USHEALTH's breaches of Sections 3.1(a) and 4.5(a), plus prejudgment interest from January 25, 2023 through judgment, compounded quarterly.

The parties agreed that Golden Rule is entitled to $38,342,458 plus prejudgment interest from January 25, 2023, that partial Rule 54(b) certification is appropriate, and that the Court should reserve jurisdiction over attorneys' fees and costs.

Golden Rule conceded SRS is entitled to prejudgment interest on the roughly $1.8 million of the Final Adjustment Amount not attributed to the breaches, which it calculated at $327,477 ($434,693 with additional interest). It proposed applying that amount only as an offset and declaring the Summary Judgment Order "satisfied and of no further effect."

Under Merger Agreement § 9.3(b)-(c), the Escrow Funds are, subject to exceptions, the sole source of recovery and exclusive remedy for indemnification. Golden Rule asserted only $44.6 million remains in escrow, which is insufficient to satisfy its judgment.
summary.practical_takeaway: A buyer that wants to withhold or net a post-closing true-up against pending indemnification claims must negotiate an express right to do so. Absent one, the true-up is due when finally determined, and prejudgment interest for late payment survives a later indemnification win, even where escrow is insufficient to cover that win. Denial of Rule 54(b) certification for an interlocutory interest award should not be read as reserving it for later revision; a party seeking revision must show a compelling reason under the law of the case.
summary.standard_of_review: Rule 54(b) partial final judgment where there is no just reason for delay. Revision of an interlocutory order under Rule 54(b) is guided by the law of the case doctrine: a prior ruling is not disturbed absent a compelling reason, such as the ruling being clearly wrong, producing an injustice, or warranting revisit because of changed circumstances. Equitable set-off is allowed only when equity and good conscience require it, substantial justice will be promoted, and third-party rights are not infringed (Pettinaro).

entries.name: PPG Industries, Inc. v. Westlake Corporation, et al.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: PPG's argument that § 2.10(a) required Spinco to cause PPG's removal as defendant: the Court noted the plain language suggests § 5.6(c) governs substitution of "Actions." In any event, PPG waived the point by not responding to Defendants' argument that any § 2.10 claim accrued in 2013 and is time-barred.

PPG's argument that the risk of enforcement against its Brazilian subsidiary, loss of Brazilian market access and reputational harm justify specific performance: rejected. Its expert testified only to a "theoretical" veil-piercing risk without knowing PPG's structure, a veil-piercing request would stay enforcement, and PPG showed no imminent threat or actual Brazil business plan.

PPG's argument that § 5.6(c) requires adding a Spinco entity as a defendant if substitution fails: rejected, because the provision's mandate is only to "endeavor to substitute" and says nothing about addition (fn. 127).

Defendants' argument, and their requested declaration, that Article V indemnification is PPG's exclusive remedy under § 5.7: rejected. Section 5.7 expressly preserves specific performance and § 7.15 equitable relief.

PPG's argument that Defendants must satisfy any Di Gregorio judgment before any assignment of insurance rights: rejected as to defense costs already paid, which triggered § 5.4(b)'s payment-against-assignment right.

Defendants' request for an immediate assignment of all insurance rights, including for any settlement or judgment: rejected. Section 5.4(b) requires payment before the assignment right arises, and a full assignment would contravene PPG's bargained-for retention of the Policies.

PPG's argument, first made at the supplemental hearing, that Defendants' Di Gregorio defense fees are not a PPG loss giving rise to insurance rights: waived. It was unbriefed and contrary to PPG's own briefed position that defense costs are reimbursable.

PPG's adoption theory against Westlake: rejected. Section 7.8 binds only successors and permitted assigns, Westlake is neither after the reverse triangular mergers, and managing the Di Gregorio defense is not adoption; Lorillard and OrbiMed are distinguished.

PPG's alter-ego theory: rejected as a matter of law. PPG never argued that Eagle US 2 is a sham existing only as a vehicle for fraud and did not address the veil-piercing factors; Westlake's running of the Di Gregorio defense is not enough.

PPG's equitable estoppel theory against Westlake: rejected on all three elements. Section 5.6(a) gave PPG the means to learn of and monitor the litigation, PPG showed no reasonable reliance beyond expecting the Spinco Group to perform, and it showed no prejudice given Defendants' defense and hold-harmless commitments. The Court did not decide whether Hallisey bars estoppel here.

authorities_cited.authority: 26 Cap. Acq. Corp. v. Tiger Resort Asia Ltd., 309 A.3d 434 (Del. Ch. 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: Specific performance requires a proven breach and a clear and convincing showing that the equities favor it; a contractual specific-performance provision supports but does not compel the decree.

authorities_cited.authority: Separation Agreement §§ 5.4(b), 6.11(a), 2.4(b)(iv)
authorities_cited.proposition: Policies are excluded assets retained by PPG. PPG must use commercially reasonable efforts to pursue Insurance Proceeds. Indemnification payments are made against an assignment of the indemnitee's "entire claim ... for Insurance Proceeds," and a "notwithstanding" anti-windfall clause bars insurers from escaping covered claims.

authorities_cited.authority: Insurance policy (JX 1) definitions of Claim, Damages and Defense Costs
authorities_cited.proposition: Defense Costs "incurred by or on behalf of the Insured" are Damages, supporting a narrow reading of "entire claim" that reaches the defense costs Defendants paid on PPG's behalf.

authorities_cited.authority: Separation Agreement §§ 5.7, 7.15
authorities_cited.proposition: Section 7.15 stipulates to specific performance. Section 5.7's exclusive-remedy clause expressly carves out specific performance and § 7.15 equitable relief.

authorities_cited.authority: Separation Agreement § 5.6(c)
authorities_cited.proposition: On request, the parties must "endeavor to substitute" the Indemnifying Party for the named defendant; the provision contains no addition mandate.

authorities_cited.authority: Separation Agreement §§ 5.5, 5.6(a)
authorities_cited.proposition: The non-managing party may be consulted on request and may retain monitoring counsel "at its own cost." This defeated PPG's estoppel theory and its claim for Brazilian monitoring fees.

authorities_cited.authority: Separation Agreement § 7.8
authorities_cited.proposition: The agreement binds only the parties and their successors and permitted assigns, which defeated PPG's adoption theory against Westlake.

authorities_cited.authority: Emerald P'rs v. Berlin, 726 A.2d 1215 (Del. 1999)
authorities_cited.proposition: Issues not briefed are deemed waived; applied to PPG's § 2.10 time-bar response and its defense-cost argument.

authorities_cited.authority: Motors Liquidation Co. DIP Lenders Tr. v. Allstate Ins. Co., 191 A.3d 1109 (Del. 2018) (TABLE)
authorities_cited.proposition: Judicial estoppel bars positions contrary to representations a court relied on; applied to Defendants' defense and hold-harmless commitments.

authorities_cited.authority: Hermelin v. K-V Pharm. Co., 2011 WL 6225377 (Del. Ch. Dec. 13, 2011)
authorities_cited.proposition: A declaratory request is mooted by a relied-on concession, which judicially estops the conceding party; applied to the assumption-of-liability declaration.

authorities_cited.authority: Nevins v. Bryan, 885 A.2d 233 (Del. Ch. 2005)
authorities_cited.proposition: Equitable estoppel requires lack of knowledge or means of knowledge, reasonable reliance and a prejudicial change of position, each proven by clear and convincing evidence.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Sunstates Corp. S'holder Litig., 788 A.2d 530 (Del. Ch. 2001) (quoting Wallace v. Wood, 752 A.2d 1175 (Del. Ch. 1999))
authorities_cited.proposition: Alter-ego veil piercing requires that the entity be a sham existing only as a vehicle for fraud.

authorities_cited.authority: Am. Legacy Found. v. Lorillard Tobacco Co., 831 A.2d 335 (Del. Ch. 2003)
authorities_cited.proposition: A non-signatory may adopt a contract only if the contract contemplates adoption. There, express provisions and the non-signatory's conduct showed adoption, unlike Westlake's.

authorities_cited.authority: OrbiMed Advisors LLC v. Symbiomix Therapeutics, LLC, 2024 WL 747567
authorities_cited.proposition: The acquirer there adopted the indemnification agreements and became a successor to substantially all of the target's assets; Westlake is not a successor.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Estate of Crist, 863 A.2d 255 (Del. Ch. 2004)
authorities_cited.proposition: A "notwithstanding" clause overrides conflicting provisions.

authorities_cited.authority: Chamison v. HealthTrust, Inc.—Hospital Co., 735 A.2d 912 (Del. Ch. 1999)
authorities_cited.proposition: A parent is not a successor-in-interest to a subsidiary that still exists.

authorities_cited.authority: Balotti & Finkelstein, Delaware Law of Corporations & Business Organizations §§ 9.7–9.8
authorities_cited.proposition: In a reverse triangular merger the target survives and its rights and obligations are not transferred.

authorities_cited.authority: 2 Pomeroy's Equity Jurisprudence § 418
authorities_cited.proposition: Equity aids the vigilant, not those who slumber on their rights.

authorities_cited.authority: Cleveland-Cliffs Burns Harbor LLC v. Boomerang Tube, LLC, 2023 WL 5688392 (Del. Ch. Sept. 5, 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: Lists the factors for disregarding the corporate form; PPG did not address them.

authorities_cited.authority: Carteret Bancorp, Inc. v. HomeGroup, Inc., 1988 WL 3010 (Del. Ch. Jan. 13, 1988)
authorities_cited.proposition: Anticipatory repudiation will not support specific performance before performance is due. Fn. 185 noted PPG's bond/payment request might be premature on this basis but did not rest on it.

authorities_cited.authority: Fortis Advisors, LLC v. Krafton, Inc., 354 A.3d 906 (Del. Ch. 2026); Martin Marietta Mat'ls, Inc. v. Vulcan Mat'ls Co., 68 A.3d 1208 (Del. 2012)
authorities_cited.proposition: Specific performance remains discretionary despite a contractual stipulation, which is honored absent a persuasive reason to disregard it.

authorities_cited.authority: Thompson St. Cap. P'rs IV, L.P. v. Sonova U.S. Hearing Instruments, LLC, 340 A.3d 1151 (Del. 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: The specific qualifies the general. Cited for Defendants' unresolved argument that failure to discharge under § 5.2(a) is not a breach.

authorities_cited.authority: Hallisey v. Artic Intermediate, LLC, 2020 WL 6438990 (Del. Ch. Oct. 29, 2020)
authorities_cited.proposition: Equitable estoppel is not the proper remedy to enforce bargained-for contract rights; the Court did not resolve its application here.

authorities_cited.authority: Roca v. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co., 842 A.2d 1238 (Del. 2004)
authorities_cited.proposition: Perfunctory, undeveloped arguments are waived.

authorities_cited.authority: Montgomery Cellular Hldg. Co. v. Dobler, 880 A.2d 206 (Del. 2005); Beck v. Atl. Coast PLC, 868 A.2d 840 (Del. Ch. 2005)
authorities_cited.proposition: The American Rule and the bad-faith exception, which requires clear evidence of vexatious conduct.
Contract parties may seek declaratory judgments; declaratory relief is discretionary and requires an actual controversy.

authorities_cited.authority: State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Spine Care Del., LLC, 238 A.3d 850 (Del. 2020)
authorities_cited.proposition: The party seeking a declaratory judgment bears the burden.

authorities_cited.authority: L-5 Healthcare P'rs, LLC v. Alphatec Hldgs., Inc., 2024 WL 3888696 (quoting Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 357, 358)
authorities_cited.proposition: A specific performance decree need not mirror the contract performance exactly. Fn. 277 used this to say the limited assignment also fits PPG's commercially-reasonable-efforts obligation.

summary.brief_summary: PPG sued Westlake, Axiall, Eagle US 2 and Eagle Spinco for specific performance compelling them to substitute into a Brazilian suit over the 1998 DG Harmony fire and to bond or pay a large Brazilian judgment; Defendants counterclaimed for an assignment of PPG's retained insurance rights. After trial, Vice Chancellor Cook assumed a breach of the duty to endeavor to substitute but held the equities weighed against any order: an order to act in, bond or pay the Brazil case would undercut a 2009 SDNY injunction against that suit and offend comity, and PPG delayed 11 years. The Court held that § 5.4(b)'s payment-against-assignment and anti-windfall provisions entitle the indemnifying Spinco entities to an assignment of PPG's claim to insurance proceeds, but only for defense costs they have already paid. It rejected PPG's adoption, alter-ego and estoppel theories against non-signatory Westlake, and denied fee shifting.
summary.core_legal_issue: Under the 2012 PPG/Eagle Spinco Separation Agreement, (i) whether PPG can obtain specific performance compelling the Spinco Group to substitute into (or join) the Brazilian Di Gregorio Litigation and to post a bond or satisfy the Brazilian judgment, where a 2009 SDNY default judgment enjoined that litigation and PPG waited 11 years after the Spinoff to request substitution; (ii) whether, and when, PPG must assign its rights to insurance proceeds covering the Di Gregorio Liability to the indemnifying Spinco entities under § 5.4(b)'s payment-against-assignment and anti-windfall language; and (iii) whether non-signatory parent Westlake is bound by the Spinco Group's obligations.
summary.holding:
After trial, PPG's requests for specific performance, Di Gregorio fees and bad-faith fee shifting were denied, and Defendants' request for specific performance was granted in part.

(1) PPG's declarations. The requested declarations that Eagle US 2 assumed the Di Gregorio Liability and bears its liabilities and defense costs present no live controversy, because Defendants conceded them. The Court relied on those concessions and held Defendants judicially estopped from contrary positions.

(2) Substitution. Assuming without deciding a breach of § 5.6(c), the Court denied substitution or addition because PPG did not show by clear and convincing evidence that the equities favor it. Ordering a Spinco entity into the Brazil case would risk making the Court complicit in circumventing the SDNY Order and would offend comity. PPG also delayed 11 years. The experts agreed addition, not substitution, was the likely result, which would give Di Gregorio another pocket. PPG's claimed harms were speculative.

(3) Bond or payment. The Court declined to decide whether Eagle US 2's failure to discharge the liability under § 2.1(b) is a breach, or whether the request is premature because no order to pay has issued (fn. 185). It denied a bond or payment order on comity grounds, adding that a bond would not stay enforcement and would expose the funds. The ruling is limited to the facts "as they currently stand," and the equities could shift (fn. 187). PPG retains its Article V indemnity.

(4) Defendants' declarations. Section 5.7 does not preclude specific performance. Westlake is not a proper defendant: it is not a successor or assign, and PPG's adoption, alter-ego and estoppel theories fail.

(5) Assignment. PPG breached § 5.4(b) by not assigning its claim for Insurance Proceeds covering the defense costs Defendants paid on PPG's behalf. The equities clearly and convincingly favor specific performance, because PPG's own witnesses supported the entitlement and its commercial reasonableness and the insurers said they would not unreasonably withhold consent. PPG must assign its right to insurance proceeds for defense costs Defendants incurred and paid; if insurer consent is required, PPG must act to effect the assignment. No assignment of all policy rights issues before payment. The Court did not further address an alternative breach of PPG's commercially-reasonable-efforts obligation (fn. 264).

(6) Fees. PPG's Brazilian monitoring-counsel fees are barred by §§ 5.5 and 5.6(a). Bad-faith fee shifting is denied because the case reflects a legitimate dispute.

The parties must submit a joint implementing order within ten business days, identifying which Defendant entity receives the assignment, and must advise the Court of any outstanding issues.
key_facts_and_concessions: The October 28, 2009 SDNY Order declared that "PPG has no liability to Di Gregorio" and expressly enjoined Di Gregorio from pursuing the Manaus, Brazil action against PPG; the Brazil court nonetheless found PPG liable (2010, final 2019) and on May 21, 2024 awarded about $90.4 million plus about $93.3 million in corrections and interest, plus fees and a fine.

PPG first demanded substitution on March 12, 2024, 11 years after the January 2013 Spinoff, though it had requested substitution in at least one other assumed-liability litigation after the Spinoff and in another lawsuit in 2021.

Defendants conceded that Eagle US 2 assumed the Di Gregorio Liability and will be responsible for any final, non-appealable judgment, and committed under oath and in filings to keep defending and to hold PPG harmless, including against enforcement of any order to pay. The Court expressly relied on these representations and held Defendants judicially estopped from contrary positions.

Defendants conceded they took no steps to substitute after PPG's 2024 request, and that § 5.6(c)'s duty to "endeavor to substitute" is enforceable by specific performance; the parties agree PPG requested substitution in 2024.

Defendants have incurred over $2 million in Di Gregorio defense fees since the Spinoff and have paid Mattos Filho, which acts under PPG's power of attorney. No order to pay had issued as of the decision, and Defendants have made no liability payment.

The insurers' January 12, 2023 letter refused to consider Westlake's invoices without an assignment from PPG and said they would not unreasonably withhold consent. PPG's insurance expert (Posner) testified that defense costs need not await satisfaction of a judgment and that a limited assignment would be commercially reasonable; PPG's Bloch testified that Defendants have a contractual entitlement to the proceeds under the anti-windfall concept.

Both Brazilian law experts agreed that posting a bond or depositing the judgment would not stay enforcement and would expose the funds to Di Gregorio. They also agreed that adding a Spinco entity is more likely than substitution and would give Di Gregorio "an extra pocket."
Westlake, a non-signatory, acquired Axiall in 2016 by reverse triangular merger (as Axiall had acquired Eagle Spinco), so Eagle US 2, Eagle Spinco and Axiall each kept its separate existence.
summary.practical_takeaway: Under a payment-against-assignment indemnity clause, an indemnitor can compel assignment of insurance proceeds only for amounts it has actually paid. Defense costs paid on the indemnitee's behalf qualify, while a judgment that has not been paid does not. Counterparties seeking specific performance of litigation-substitution rights in a spinoff should invoke them promptly, since the Court weighed PPG's 11-year delay against relief. Requests to compel action in a foreign proceeding that a U.S. court has enjoined face a heavy comity barrier.
summary.standard_of_review: Post-trial; facts stipulated or proven by a preponderance. Specific performance requires a proven breach and a clear and convincing showing that the balance of the equities favors the remedy, even with a contractual specific-performance stipulation. The party seeking a declaratory judgment bears the burden. Equitable estoppel requires clear and convincing evidence. Bad-faith fee shifting requires 'clear evidence.'
